## Context

**What this card is.** Criterion 13 asks for AI-driven incident response with a bounded
autonomy boundary. A boundary written as a paragraph is a review opinion; this card turns
it into a machine-readable artifact and gives the response loop its two executable steps:
how to roll back, and how to PROVE recovery. The three files are the whole envelope:
`incident-response/autonomy-policy.yaml` (the authority),
`incident-response/runbooks/rollback.sh` (the gated rollback step) and
`incident-response/runbooks/verify-recovery.sh` (the recovery measurement). This card
ships no incident record, no responder prompt, no schema and no collector change.

**The recovery condition is a merged contract, not an invention.**
`backend/app/routers/health.py` (read at groom, lines 40-46) computes
`fallback_active = is_fallback()` and returns `status="degraded" if fallback_active else "ok"` -
so `status == "ok"` and `fallback_active == false` are two views of ONE real payload, and
`openapi.yaml`'s `HealthResponse` component (lines 216-243, FROZEN this milestone) pins the
field names and the `ok`/`degraded` enum. ac4 therefore drives the script over served
payloads that include the two CONTRADICTORY shapes (`ok`+`true`, `degraded`+`false`) that a
script asserting only one field would wrongly accept - those two mutants are the proof that
this card asserts the conjunction rather than a wish.

**Measured base state (measured at groom at BASE 1fe7237, not assumed).**
`incident-response/` holds exactly `README.md` and `collect-evidence.sh` (t80's merged
pair); `incident-response/runbooks/` does not exist; none of this card's three files exists.
`docs/state/merge_test_index.json` holds 280 stored gates and ZERO of them name
`autonomy-policy`, `runbooks/`, `rollback.sh` as this card's surface or `verify-recovery`
(the four index entries containing the word "rollback" are t39's `ops/runbook.md` fences,
which this card's delta leaves byte-clean). There is therefore no pin switchover and no
index edit for this card. The validator pair this card pins is `python3` + PyYAML (measured:
python3 3.12.3, PyYAML 6.0.1 under WSL; PyYAML is also a committed dependency of the
backend lockfile), the same pair the merged t76 fences pin for YAML authority files - and
`node_modules/` is gitignored and measured absent in this worktree, so no node/yaml library
is pinned anywhere in these fences. `core.autocrlf=true` is set repo-wide and
`.gitattributes` is absent (both measured at groom), which is why ac5 checks the WORKING
COPY for CRLF and non-ASCII on files that are NEW in this delta (the disclosed difference
from t80's blob-level leg).

**The pinned endpoint and the fence's own dead port.** The recovery step reads the pinned
local verification endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:8137/api/v1/health` - the same
`DIAGNOSIS_ENDPOINT` row the merged t41 gate fences in
`docs/criteria/security_ops_verification.md:65` - and an argument may override it, with a
NON-loopback override REFUSED before any request. ac4's unreachable leg uses
`127.0.0.1:55901`, the FENCE's own un-listening probe port (measured dead at groom:
`curl -s -m 2 http://127.0.0.1:55901/api/v1/health` fails), chosen in the t80 ac1/ac3 style
so no later card invents another. t80's own dead ports 55432/55433 are NOT reused here, and
nothing this card writes starts a server or binds a port: the runbooks READ an endpoint that
someone else owns. The ac4 probe serves its synthetic payloads from `127.0.0.1` on an
ephemeral port that the OS assigns and that the probe itself closes - it is fence
scaffolding, never a product surface, never a pinned port, and it carries a health payload
shaped by `openapi.yaml`, not a secret or a real service.

**Single-source doctrine and the cross-card boundaries (hard, stated rather than fenced
where the fence would have to read another card's file).**

- **This card's envelope is exactly `autonomy-policy.yaml` + `rollback.sh` +
  `verify-recovery.sh`.** Nothing else.

**Why the deny list must be explicit, and how ac1 proves it.** A policy that lists only
allows implies its denies, and an implied deny is not a boundary - so ac1 requires three
named deny entries (`restart_production`, `database_mutation`, `merge`), each carrying a
reason and at least three concrete forbidden command shapes, plus
`default_decision: deny` AND `unknown_action_decision: deny` so an unnamed action cannot be
defaulted into permission. The leg is non-vacuous by construction: ac1's probe REJECTS a
synthetic allow-only policy, a synthetic `default_decision: allow` policy, and a policy that
lists the same id in both lists. **Why an allow needs a scope, and how ac2 proves it.** An
allow that does not say which paths may be written or which endpoints may be read is a gap
wearing a permission, so ac2 requires every allow entry to carry a scope sentence of real
length, requires every read endpoint to match a loopback regex, requires the read class to
cover at least two reads (log AND metric, per the card's own wording), requires the
report-writing class to name writable paths relative to the repository root and to name
`.env` and `~/.ssh` in its `forbidden_paths`, and rejects a synthetic unscoped allow, a
synthetic `http://metrics.internal:9090/...` endpoint and a synthetic allow list with no
report-writing class at all.

**The policy's deny list expressed as a test (ac3).** ac3 greps the two scripts for the
denied command classes on NON-comment lines only (a comment naming a denial is the point of
a comment): merge/rebase/push/`--force`, SQL DML and DDL, `docker`/`docker-compose`/
`kubectl`/`systemctl`/`service restart`/`pkill`/`kill -9`/`sudo`, and the server-starters
`http.server`/`uvicorn` (a runbook that starts a server would bind a port, which the card
forbids). It also scans every URL authority in non-comment lines against
`{127.0.0.1, localhost}`. The scan's own bite is proven by feeding it a synthetic script
carrying `git merge`, a SQL `UPDATE` and `http://metrics.internal:9090/...` and requiring
three hits.

**`rollback.sh` is honest about what a rollback is here (the card's own constraint).** This
repository owns no production orchestrator, so an automated rollback would be a fake. The
script therefore REQUIRES three things before it prints anything - an explicit `--target`,
an explicit `--image` reference, and a `--i-am-human` operator flag - and then prints a
plan whose steps are "confirm the previous image against the deployment record" and
"redeploy that reference through the tooling that owns that target", followed by "prove
recovery with `verify-recovery.sh`". It executes none of them, opens no connection, and
writes nothing (ac3 proves the last by running it inside a freshly created empty directory
and requiring that directory to still be empty). The printed plan names
`incident-response/autonomy-policy.yaml` as the authority and states that a redeployment is
OUTSIDE `allowed_actions`, so a responder that runs the script without a human is out of
policy even when the arguments parse - the gate is a floor, not a permission.

**Environment honesty (the t65/t81 lessons, measured at groom).** This worktree's gitdir
holds Windows-formatted paths, so every git read in ac5 goes through
`cmd.exe /c "git -C <wslpath -w form> ..."` with `</dev/null` INSIDE the bash side (never a
`2>&1` or `&` inside a cmd.exe string - the cmd separator trap) and output `tr -d "\r"`
stripped; the fence REDs loudly if `cmd.exe` is missing rather than skipping the purity leg.
The fences themselves run under WSL bash and need only `bash`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `tr`,
`wc`, `mktemp`, `base64`, `curl`, `python3` (stdlib `json`/`re`/`sys` + PyYAML for the two
policy probes) and `cmd.exe` + `wslpath`. Every probe is materialised at run time from a
base64 literal inside the fence, so the fence body carries zero single quotes, zero
backticks, zero tabs and exactly one line - the t76/t81 fence shape. No fence installs
anything, downloads anything, or touches Docker.

**Granularity honesty.** max_files=4 and this card uses exactly 3. max_acs=6 and this card
uses 5. max_diff_lines=300 is warn-only and the groom's throwaway candidate measured **349
added lines** across the three files (policy 166, rollback 91, verify-recovery 92), so the
cap WILL be exceeded: a policy with explicit reasoned denies plus scoped allows plus two
gated scripts is what "the boundary is a machine-readable artifact and recovery is a
measured claim" costs. ac5 prints the measured number and a WARN, and the handoff discloses
the exceedance rather than trimming a mechanism the card scoped.

**Review_plan disposition.** The phase_13 review_plan verdict is PASS_WITH_WARNINGS; what it

## Acceptance criteria

Five criteria - within max_acs=6. Each is one deterministic `bash -c` one-liner run from the
repository root (worktree). All five were EXECUTED at base 1fe7237 by this groom and are RED
there for the named reason (see the table under **Verification commands**). Every fence is
GREEN-able: all five were re-executed against a throwaway candidate (three scratch files
staged under the gitignored `build/t82/cand/` tree and copied into place, then removed), and
five deliberate mutants were each REJECTED; the groom wrote NO product content into the
project tree and committed nothing. No fence needs Docker, an internet connection, an
install step, a live backend, or the `/metrics` endpoint to be implemented.

### ac1 - the policy exists, parses, and DENIES the three forbidden action classes by name

`incident-response/autonomy-policy.yaml` exists and parses under the pinned validator pair
(`python3` + PyYAML, the merged t76 pair, no node fallback). An embedded probe asserts the
deny side of the boundary: `denied_actions` is a non-empty list whose entries each carry an
`id`, a non-empty `reason` and at least three concrete `forbidden_commands`; the three
denied classes are named individually (`restart`, `database`+`mutation`, `merge`);
`default_decision` AND `unknown_action_decision` are both `deny`, so an action the policy
never names cannot be defaulted into permission; no action id appears in BOTH lists; and the
fallback signal is CITED, never redefined - every line naming `db_fallback_active` must also
name `observability/alerts.yaml` or the word `source`, because t76 owns that name. The
negative controls are the point: the same legs must REJECT a synthetic allow-only policy, a
synthetic `default_decision: allow` policy, and a policy that denies and allows the same id.

### ac2 - the policy ALLOWS exactly the two permitted action classes, each with its scope

The same file's `allowed_actions` must admit exactly two classes - `read_only_reads` and
`report_writing` - and no third class. Every entry carries a scope sentence of real length
(an allow with no scope is a gap, not a permission); every read endpoint matches a loopback
regex and every read method is `GET` or a file read; the read class covers at least two
reads so both log and metric reads are inside the boundary; the report-writing allow names
writable paths that are relative to the repository root and lists `.env` and `~/.ssh` among
its `forbidden_paths` (the coding-standards forbidden-actions table, stated on the write
scope rather than assumed). Three negative controls prove the legs bite: a synthetic
unscoped allow, a synthetic `http://metrics.internal:9090/...` read endpoint, and a synthetic
allow list with no `report_writing` class must each be REJECTED.

### ac4 - verify-recovery.sh asserts the REAL recovery condition and fails otherwise

The script exits 0 ONLY when the health payload says `status == "ok"` AND
`fallback_active == false`, and exits non-zero with a readable reason otherwise. The proof is
driven, not asserted: the fence first MEASURES that its dead probe port `127.0.0.1:55901` is
un-listening, then serves four payloads from a loopback ephemeral port and requires the exact
pass/fail pattern of all of them plus two more runs - `ok`+`fallback_active:true` must FAIL
(a script asserting only `status` would wrongly pass it), `degraded`+`false` must FAIL (a
script asserting only `fallback_active` would wrongly pass it), `degraded`+`true` must FAIL,
a non-JSON body must FAIL, the measured-dead endpoint must FAIL with an `unreachable`
message, a non-loopback URL must be REFUSED with a `loopback` message, and
`ok`+`false` must be ACCEPTED printing `RECOVERY_VERIFIED` (the positive control). A skipped
read may never count as recovery: missing `curl` or `python3` REDs the fence.

